name: Cloud Cost Management
intent: Pay only for capacity that does work: size servers to what they use, follow the load instead of the peak, commit to the steady base, run bursts on spare capacity, and switch off what nobody uses.
scenario: A web service needs between 3 and 16 servers depending on the hour, plus a 6-server test environment. It runs on large servers that are half idle, kept at peak size all day, all paid on demand, with the test environment on day and night: $7,488 a month. The same traffic is then served more cheaply, one change at a time.
problem: In the cloud every idle server is billed by the hour, and nobody gets an error when money is wasted. Fleets are sized for the busiest hour and left that way, servers are bigger than the app needs, test environments run all weekend, and discounts are either ignored or bought for more than you use. The bill grows quietly, and by the time someone looks, nobody remembers why each resource exists.

howItWorks.title: See where the money goes
howItWorks.text: Tag every resource with its team, service and environment, so the bill can be split and each owner sees their share. Measure utilization: how much of what you pay for does work. A fleet that is busy a quarter of the time is paying four times what it needs.

howItWorks.title: Right-size
howItWorks.text: Pick the instance size from what the service actually uses (CPU, memory) at its busiest, with some margin, not from a guess made at launch. A server twice as big as needed costs twice as much and does the same work. Check again after big changes, because usage drifts.

howItWorks.title: Follow the load
howItWorks.text: Traffic rises and falls through the day. Autoscaling runs enough servers for the current load plus headroom, instead of enough for the peak all day long. The quiet hours, often more than half the day, stop costing peak prices.

howItWorks.title: Commit to the base, burst on spare capacity
howItWorks.text: Providers sell discounts (reserved instances, savings plans, committed use) for promising to pay for some capacity every hour for a year or more, used or not. Commit only to the level you never go below. Above it, spot or preemptible capacity is far cheaper but can be taken back at short notice, so use it for stateless servers that can be replaced.

howItWorks.title: Switch off what nobody uses
howItWorks.text: Test and development environments, forgotten experiments, unattached disks and old snapshots cost money while doing nothing. Schedule non-production to stop outside working hours, delete what has no owner, and set budgets with alerts, so a surprise shows up in days, not at the end of the month.

pros: Large savings without changing the product: here the same traffic costs 84% less
Utilization and tagging also show which services are inefficient or unowned
Autoscaling and schedules save money and also adapt to growth on their own
Budgets and alerts catch mistakes (a runaway job, a forgotten cluster) in days
cons: Commitments are bets: over-commit and you pay for capacity you never use
Spot capacity can disappear at short notice, so it needs replaceable, stateless work
Autoscaling needs warm-up time and good metrics, or a sudden spike hits a fleet that is too small
Cutting too close removes the headroom that keeps latency low during spikes
whenToUse: Any cloud bill large enough that someone asks about it
Traffic that varies through the day or week
Many teams sharing one account, where nobody owns the total
whenNotToUse: Committing to capacity before you know your steady usage: measure for a few weeks first
Spot capacity for stateful databases or work that cannot be interrupted
Squeezing a small bill where the engineering time costs more than the savings
pitfalls: Buying a commitment for the peak instead of the base, so the quiet hours are paid for anyway
Rightsizing on average usage, so the busy hour runs out of CPU or memory
No tags, so the bill cannot be split and nobody feels responsible
Forgetting data transfer, storage and log volume, which can rival compute
Spot fleets with no fallback, so a reclaim wave becomes an outage
Test environments, snapshots and disks that outlive the project they were made for

quiz.question: A service autoscales on demand from 4 servers at night to 16 at its daily peak, about 10 on average. The team buys a one-year commitment for 20 servers, assuming a 40% discount. What happens to the bill?
options: It drops by 40%, because every server now has the discount.
It drops a little, because only the peak hours get cheaper.
It stays the same, because commitments only change how the bill is shown.
It rises: idle committed servers are paid for all night and most of the day.
quiz.explanation: A commitment is paid every hour, used or not. 20 committed servers at 60% of the price cost as much as 12 on-demand servers running all day, more than the 10 the autoscaled fleet averages. Commit to the level you never go below, and cover the rest with on-demand or spot capacity.

quiz.question: A fleet's servers use about 40% of their CPU at the busiest hour. What is the best first step?
options: Buy a commitment for the current fleet, since it is clearly needed.
Move to a smaller size that still leaves some headroom at the busiest hour.
Move every server to spot capacity, because it is the cheapest option.
Add more servers, because low CPU means the requests are waiting on I/O.
quiz.explanation: Rightsizing comes first: committing to oversized servers locks the waste in for a year. Sizing from the busy hour, with a margin, keeps latency safe. Spot does not fix oversizing and adds reclaim risk, and adding servers does nothing about idle CPU.

quiz.question: Which workload is the best fit for spot or preemptible capacity?
options: The primary database, which holds every customer order and takes all the writes.
A leader-elected scheduler that has to stay up and must never be interrupted.
Stateless web servers above the base load, behind a load balancer.
A single server that holds user sessions in its own memory between requests.
quiz.explanation: Spot capacity can be taken back with little warning. Stateless servers behind a load balancer can lose an instance without losing data, and on-demand capacity can replace it. Databases, singletons and servers holding in-memory state lose work when reclaimed.
